# ML-1 results — generated by `train.py`, not hand-edited

Generated in 17.7 min of CPU wall time.


## 1. Benchmark: all four sub-datasets

Test-set protocol: one prediction per test unit, at its last available cycle,
scored against `RUL_FDxxx.txt` clipped at the 125-cycle cap (the protocol the
quoted papers use). PHM score is the asymmetric C-MAPSS/PHM08 sum — lower is
better, and it is a SUM, so it scales with the number of test units.

| sub-dataset | conditions | fault modes | units (tr/ho/te) | GBM RMSE | GBM PHM | LSTM RMSE | LSTM PHM | lit. best RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 | 1 | 1 | 80/20/100 | 12.03 | 216 | 14.34 | 413 | 12.61 |
| FD002 | 6 | 1 | 240/20/259 | 13.17 | 794 | 17.15 | 2198 | 22.36 |
| FD003 | 1 | 2 | 80/20/100 | 12.77 | 289 | 15.25 | 1198 | 12.64 |
| FD004 | 6 | 2 | 229/20/248 | 14.48 | 1052 | 15.26 | 1147 | 23.31 |

Published reference points (quoted, **not** reproduced here):

| method | FD001 | FD002 | FD003 | FD004 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LSTM (Zheng 2017) | 16.14 / 338 | 24.49 / 4450 | 16.18 / 852 | 28.17 / 5550 |
| DCNN (Li 2018) | 12.61 / 273 | 22.36 / 10412 | 12.64 / 284 | 23.31 / 12466 |

**The gap.** Best-model RMSE is +2.45 worse on FD004 than on FD001. FD004 flies 6 operating conditions against FD001's 1, and carries two fault modes rather than one. Condition normalisation (`cmapss.ConditionNormaliser`) removes the first difference — it is why 16 sensors survive the variance screen on FD004 versus 14 on FD001. What is left is the second: a single model is averaging two degradation physics, and closing that needs either a fault-mode classifier upstream or a mixture head. Neither is built here.

## 2. Where the error lives (horizon-stratified)

Computed on held-out run-to-failure units, all cycles — not on the censored test set.

| sub-dataset | [0,20) | [20,50) | [50,90) | [90,126) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 RMSE | 3.3 | 9.3 | 17.9 | 9.8 |
| FD002 RMSE | 3.7 | 9.7 | 16.1 | 14.0 |
| FD003 RMSE | 2.9 | 7.0 | 14.3 | 10.0 |
| FD004 RMSE | 8.6 | 15.8 | 25.1 | 14.3 |

The shape is not monotonic and should not be read as if it were. On FD001 the error is lowest near failure (3.3 in `[0,20)`), peaks in the `[50,90)` band at 17.9, and falls again in `[90,126)` (9.8). Two different things are happening. The far band is easy for an uninteresting reason: the 125-cycle cap makes early life a constant, and predicting a constant is free — that band's low error is an artefact of the target, not evidence of skill. The middle band is genuinely the hardest region, where degradation has become visible but has not yet become decisive.

The band that matters is `[0,20)`, and it is the best one (3.3 RMSE, bias +1.0). That is the property to argue for: the alarm decision is taken in the last few dozen cycles of life, so accuracy is being spent where it converts into a maintenance date. A model with the same aggregate RMSE and the opposite profile would be useless, and no aggregate number would say so.

## 3. Prognostic horizon (α-λ, α = 0.2)

*Converged* means the prediction entered the accuracy cone and never left it again. Entering **and staying** is the requirement; a model that dips into the cone and back out has not converged, and any snapshot metric would credit it anyway.

Two cones. **Strict** is ±0.2·RUL exactly as defined. **Floored** is ±max(0.2·RUL, 5 cycles). The gap between the two columns is the finding — see below.

| sub-dataset | converged (floored) | converged (strict) | median PH, cycles | median λ | α-λ accuracy at λ=0.5 | at λ=0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 | 20/20 | 1/20 | 15 | 0.91 | 75% | 80% |
| FD002 | 17/20 | 4/20 | 12 | 0.95 | 65% | 70% |
| FD003 | 20/20 | 6/20 | 16 | 0.92 | 75% | 80% |
| FD004 | 12/20 | 2/20 | 2 | 0.98 | 80% | 35% |

**Read the two columns together.** Under the strict cone, 13/80 units converge. Under the floored cone, 69/80. That collapse is not the model getting worse — it is the metric. The strict cone at RUL = 3 demands the prediction land within 0.6 of a cycle *and never leave*, which no prognostic on any sensor suite achieves, so strict PH is close to a constant zero for everyone and discriminates nothing. The floor of 5 cycles encodes a maintenance fact: once RUL is inside a week, the difference between Tuesday and Wednesday no longer changes the plan, because the work order is already cut.

I am reporting both rather than the flattering one. If a reviewer prefers the strict definition, the strict column is the answer and it is bad — and the reason it is bad is worth more in an interview than the floored number is.

## 4. The alarm policy — what a planner actually buys

| sub-dataset | policy | mean lead | P05 lead | ≥10 cycles | missed | nuisance alarms / unit-life |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FD001 | RUL<25, k=5 | 16.9 | 12 | 100% | 0% | 0.05 |
| FD002 | RUL<30, k=8 | 20.4 | 15 | 100% | 0% | 0.00 |
| FD003 | RUL<25, k=8 | 14.4 | 12 | 100% | 0% | 0.00 |
| FD004 | RUL<45, k=8 | 28.9 | 18 | 100% | 0% | 0.30 |

FD001, in the sentence a maintenance manager reads: **we alert 17 cycles early on average, 100% of units get at least 10 cycles of warning, and the operator sees 0.05 alarms per engine-life that clear on their own.**

### Why k=5? The persistence curve (FD001, threshold fixed at 25)

| k | mean lead | missed | nuisance / unit-life | cost per unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20.9 | 0% | 0.65 | 1.544 |
| 2 | 19.9 | 0% | 0.25 | 1.324 |
| 3 | 18.9 | 0% | 0.10 | 1.229 |
| 5 | 16.9 | 0% | 0.05 | 1.164 |
| 8 | 14.5 | 10% | 0.00 | 2.981 |
| 12 | 12.3 | 45% | 0.00 | 9.575 |

Raising k trades lead time (you wait k cycles before asserting) against nuisance alarms. The curve is the answer to "why 3?" — it is not 3 because 3 is a nice number, it is whichever k minimises the cost column, and the column is visible so the planner can disagree with the cost model rather than with the number.

### Sensitivity: does the operating point survive different cost assumptions?

Two axes, because they pull in opposite directions: `c_fail` (cost of an in-service failure) wants the alarm earlier, `c_life` (cost per cycle of remaining life discarded by pulling early) wants it later.

| axis | value | chosen threshold | k | mean lead | missed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `c_fail` | 5:1 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_fail` | 10:1 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_fail` | 20:1 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_fail` | 50:1 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_fail` | 100:1 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_life` | 0.00 | RUL<35 | 8 | 21.9 | 0% |
| `c_life` | 0.02 | RUL<25 | 5 | 16.9 | 0% |
| `c_life` | 0.10 | RUL<15 | 1 | 12.8 | 0% |
| `c_life` | 0.30 | RUL<15 | 1 | 12.8 | 0% |
| `c_life` | 1.00 | RUL<15 | 1 | 12.8 | 0% |

**The `c_fail` axis is flat** — the same policy (RUL<25, k=5) wins from 5:1 to 100:1. That is not the sweep failing, it is the sweep telling me which constraint is binding. At the chosen persistence 0% of units are missed, so the `c_fail` term contributes nothing to the objective and multiplying it by 20 multiplies zero. The policy is robust to the number I am least able to source, which is the good version of this result — but it is robust because it is not being tested, and saying only 'insensitive to failure cost' would have been misleading.

The `c_life` axis is where the policy actually moves: the threshold goes from RUL<35 at c_life=0.00 to RUL<15 at c_life=1.00, and mean lead time falls from 21.9 to 12.8 cycles. So the number to go and get from finance is not the cost of a failure — it is **what an hour of unused remaining life is worth**, which is the one nobody asks for.

## 5. The RUL cap — how much does 125 matter?

GBM on FD001, refit per cap. The first two columns score each model against its own capped truth and are **not** comparable across rows — a lower cap compresses the target and flatters itself. The last two columns restrict scoring to the 54 test units with true RUL ≤ 90, a range every cap can express — which removes *some* of that unfairness but, as the discussion below works through, not all of it.

| cap | RMSE (own truth) | PHM (own truth) | RMSE (RUL≤90) | PHM (RUL≤90) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 90 | 6.50 | 58 | 7.40 | 42 |
| 110 | 9.33 | 122 | 9.79 | 77 |
| 125 | 12.03 | 216 | 10.41 | 92 |
| 140 | 14.33 | 364 | 11.00 | 113 |
| 200 | 20.60 | 1748 | 13.88 | 287 |
| none | 23.46 | 4864 | 17.38 | 2297 |

**The clearest result is the uncapped row.** It scores 17.38 RMSE / 2297 PHM against 7.40 / 42 for the best capped model — a 54× worse PHM score, and PHM is the metric that weights the end of life where the alarm decision is taken. An uncapped linear target asks the model to distinguish RUL 300 from RUL 250 on evidence that does not exist, and the only way to reduce that loss is to regress on cycle count — i.e. to learn the training set's censoring pattern rather than degradation.

**Among the capped rows the comparison is NOT clean, and I am not going to pretend it is.** RMSE rises monotonically with the cap (7.40 at cap 90 to 13.88 at cap 200), which looks like an argument for the lowest cap. It is not. The evaluation subset is the units with true RUL ≤ 90, and a cap-90 model is structurally unable to over-predict on that subset — the cap encodes the same prior the subset selects on. Restricting to a low-RUL region does not remove the advantage a low cap has there, it hands it over.

There is no single fixed truth on which caps compare neutrally, because the cap changes what the model is allowed to say. **The cap-neutral test is the decision layer** — refit the alarm policy per cap and compare lead time, missed rate and nuisance alarms, all of which live below RUL 50 where every cap can express the answer. That is not run here, and it is the experiment I would want before defending a cap value to anyone. What this table does support is the strong claim, which is about capping versus not capping at all.

## 6. Edge deployment — could this run on the gateway?

LSTM, 62,081 parameters, single-sample inference, onnxruntime pinned to **one** CPU thread to stand in for a gateway core.

| artefact | size | p50 latency | p99 latency | RUL delta vs fp32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PyTorch weights | 243 KB | — | — | — |
| ONNX fp32 | 247 KB | 0.17 ms | 0.57 ms | — |
| ONNX int8 (dynamic) | 73 KB | 0.15 ms | 0.50 ms | MAE 0.23 cycles, max 3.14 |

int8 costs 0.23 cycles of mean absolute disagreement with fp32. Against a lead time measured in tens of cycles that is affordable; against the ±20% α-λ cone near end of life it is not free, and the honest reading is that the size win matters more than the latency win here — an engine cycle is minutes, so neither number is a constraint. The constraint this table actually answers is memory footprint on a gateway already running protocol drivers.

---
*Every number above is a property of C-MAPSS, a simulation. See `docs/DEPLOYMENT_REALITY.md` before believing any of it about a real fleet.*
